claim: The nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS) is a key gateway for meal-related signals entering the brain from the periphery.
source: The nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS) is a key gateway for meal-related signals entering the brain from the periphery.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: A subset of NTS neurons containing cholecystokinin (CCKNTS) is responsive to nutritional state.
source: We reveal that a subset of NTS neurons containing cholecystokinin (CCKNTS) is responsive to nutritional state
evidence: Supported by c-Fos immunoreactivity data shown in Figure 1D,E,F demonstrating CCKNTS neuron activation in response to feeding and nutrient gavage.

claim: Activation of CCKNTS neurons reduces appetite in mice.
source: We reveal that a subset of NTS neurons containing cholecystokinin (CCKNTS) is responsive to nutritional state and that their activation reduces appetite and body weight in mice.
evidence: Supported by chemogenetic (DREADD) and optogenetic experiments showing reduced food intake upon CCKNTS neuron activation (Figures 2E, 2F, 3G, 3J).

claim: Activation of CCKNTS neurons reduces body weight in mice.
source: We reveal that a subset of NTS neurons containing cholecystokinin (CCKNTS) is responsive to nutritional state and that their activation reduces appetite and body weight in mice.
evidence: Supported by repeated CNO administration experiments showing body weight reduction (Figure 2J).

claim: CCKNTS neurons provide a distinctive innervation of the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH).
source: Cell-specific anterograde tracing revealed that CCKNTS neurons provide a distinctive innervation of the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH)
evidence: Supported by anterograde tracing using ChR2-eYFP showing CCKNTS projections to PVH (Figure 3C).

claim: CCKNTS fibers and varicosities are in close apposition to a subset of melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4RPVH) cells.
source: Cell-specific anterograde tracing revealed that CCKNTS neurons provide a distinctive innervation of the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH), with fibers and varicosities in close apposition to a subset of melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4RPVH) cells
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing CCKNTS fibers near MC4R-GFP neurons (Figure 3M).

claim: MC4RPVH cells are responsive to CCK.
source: Cell-specific anterograde tracing revealed that CCKNTS neurons provide a distinctive innervation of the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH), with fibers and varicosities in close apposition to a subset of melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4RPVH) cells, which are also responsive to CCK.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology showing MC4R PVH neurons are excited by CCK-8 application (Figure 3N, Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).

claim: The satiating function of CCKNTS neurons is mediated by a CCKNTS→PVH pathway.
source: Optogenetic activation of CCKNTS axon terminals within the PVH reveal the satiating function of CCKNTS neurons to be mediated by a CCKNTS→PVH pathway
evidence: Supported by optogenetic stimulation of CCKNTS terminals in PVH reducing food intake (Figure 3G, 3J).

claim: The CCKNTS→PVH pathway encodes positive valence.
source: Optogenetic activation of CCKNTS axon terminals within the PVH reveal the satiating function of CCKNTS neurons to be mediated by a CCKNTS→PVH pathway that also encodes positive valence.
evidence: Supported by real-time place preference and T-maze tests showing preference for photostimulation-paired chambers in food-deprived mice (Figure 4B, 4E).

claim: Common obesity is primarily a consequence of food intake beyond the body's energetic requirements.
source: Common obesity is primarily a consequence of food intake beyond the body's energetic requirements, with the excess energy consequently stored as fat.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The brain integrates and responds to multiple homeostatic hormones, neurotransmitters, nutrients and peripherally generated neural signals to maintain energetic balance.
source: Mechanistically, the brain integrates and responds to multiple homeostatic hormones, neurotransmitters, nutrients and peripherally generated neural signals to maintain energetic balance (Dietrich and Horvath, 2013; Morton et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: One of the primary integration nodes within the brain for meal-related and metabolic signals from the periphery is the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS).
source: One of the primary integration nodes within the brain for meal-related and metabolic signals from the periphery is the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS) (Grill and Hayes, 2012; Rinaman, 2010; Schwartz, 2010; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The NTS hosts a variety of factors to control homeostatic functions, including a small subset of neurons that express cholecystokinin (CCKNTS).
source: The NTS hosts a variety of factors to control homeostatic functions, including a small subset of neurons that express cholecystokinin (CCKNTS) (Garfield et al., 2012; Herbert and Saper, 1990; Vitale et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CCK consists of a family of peptides, the best characterized of which is a 33 amino acid peptide secreted from endocrine cells in the jejunum in response to nutrients in the intestinal lumen.
source: CCK consists of a family of peptides, the best characterized of which is a 33 amino acid peptide secreted from endocrine cells in the jejunum in response to nutrients in the intestinal lumen.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CCK.

claim: Gut-derived CCK has a number of gastrointestinal (GI) functions including the promotion of satiation/satiety.
source: This gut-derived peptide has a number of gastrointestinal (GI) functions including the promotion of satiation/satiety (Gibbs et al., 1973; Saito et al., 1981; Smith and Gibbs, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Peripherally derived CCK does not readily penetrate the brain.
source: Peripherally derived CCK does not readily penetrate the brain (Fan et al., 1997; Passaro et al., 1982).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The short-term effect of peripheral CCK on appetite has been in part attributed to stimulation of vagal sensory neurons influencing the brainstem.
source: However, its short-term effect on appetite has been in part attributed to stimulation of vagal sensory neurons influencing the brainstem (Fan et al., 1997; Gibbs et al., 1973; Saito et al., 1981; Smith and Gibbs, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CCK is synthesized within the brain, where it is post-translationally processed into an 8 amino acid peptide (CCK-8).
source: CCK is also synthesized within the brain, where it is post-translationally processed into an 8 amino acid peptide (CCK-8)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about brain CCK.

claim: CCK-8 reduces food intake when centrally infused.
source: CCK is also synthesized within the brain, where it is post-translationally processed into an 8 amino acid peptide (CCK-8) that reduces food intake when centrally infused (Blevins et al., 2000; Hirosue et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The source of brain CCK that controls appetite has not been established.
source: However, the source of brain CCK that controls appetite has not been established.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: No direct functional assessment of CCKNTS neurons has yet been undertaken.
source: although, no direct functional assessment of CCKNTS neurons has yet been undertaken.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: CCK-eYFP cells were most abundantly expressed within the caudal aspect of the NTS.
source: CCK-eYFP cells were most abundantly expressed within the caudal aspect of the NTS (Figure 1B,C)
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification in CckYFP mice (Figure 1B,C).

claim: The caudal NTS is a brain region innervated by gastrointestinal vagal afferents and involved in nutrient sensing.
source: a brain region innervated by gastrointestinal vagal afferents and involved in nutrient sensing (Appleyard et al., 2005; Blouet and Schwartz, 2012; Ritter, 2011; Schwarz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ingestion of food on an empty stomach significantly increased c-Fos-IR within CCKNTS cells.
source: In contrast to light cycle ad libitum fed and the dark cycle fasted conditions, ingestion of food on an empty stomach significantly increased c-Fos-IR within CCKNTS cells, indicating responsiveness to food consumption (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by c-Fos immunoreactivity data comparing fed, fasted, and refed conditions (Figure 1D,E).

claim: Gavage of sucrose or amino acids significantly increased c-Fos-IR within CCKNTS cells compared with water.
source: As observed with chow intake, gavage of sucrose or amino acids significantly increased c-Fos-IR within CCKNTS cells compared with water (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by c-Fos immunoreactivity data following intragastric nutrient delivery (Figure 1F).

claim: CCKNTS cells are activated by nutrient intake.
source: These results suggest that CCKNTS cells are activated by nutrient intake.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the c-Fos data showing activation following nutrient gavage.

claim: CNO activated Cck-iCre-hM3Dq-mCherryNTS cells in vivo as shown by increased c-Fos-IR.
source: CNO activated Cck-iCre-hM3Dq-mCherryNTS cells in vivo as shown by increased c-Fos-IR (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by c-Fos immunoreactivity data following CNO administration (Figure 2C).

claim: CNO activated Cck-iCre-hM3Dq-mCherryNTS cells ex vivo using electrophysiology in NTS slices.
source: CNO activated Cck-iCre-hM3Dq-mCherryNTS cells in vivo as shown by increased c-Fos-IR (Figure 2C) and ex vivo using electrophysiology in NTS slices (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing increased membrane potential and firing rate upon CNO application (Figure 2D).

claim: Activation of CCKNTS neurons in ad libitum fed Cck-iCre-hM3Dq-mCherryNTS mice injected with CNO suppressed food intake for 24 hr.
source: Activation of CCKNTS neurons in ad libitum fed Cck-iCre-hM3Dq-mCherryNTS mice injected with CNO (0.3 mg kg-1, IP) suppressed food intake for 24 hr (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by food intake measurements following CNO administration (Figure 2E).

claim: CCKNTS neuron activation suppressed re-feeding in food deprived mice.
source: Likewise, CCKNTS neuron activation suppressed re-feeding in food deprived mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by food intake measurements following CNO administration in fasted mice (Figure 2F).

claim: CCK-A receptors are downstream effectors of CCKNTS neuron-mediated reduction in feeding.
source: These results demonstrate CCK-A receptors as downstream effectors of CCKNTS neuron-mediated reduction in feeding.
evidence: Supported by devazepide (CCK-A receptor antagonist) blunting CNO-induced appetite suppression (Figure 2G).

claim: Chemogenetic activation of CCKNTS neurons in Cck-iCre-hM3Dq-mCherryNTS mice altered neither circulating blood glucose levels nor glucose disposal following a systemic glucose load.
source: Unlike CCKPBN neurons, chemogenetic activation of CCKNTS neurons in Cck-iCre-hM3Dq-mCherryNTS mice altered neither circulating blood glucose levels (Figure 2H) nor glucose disposal following a systemic glucose load (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by glucose measurements and glucose tolerance test data (Figure 2H, 2I).

claim: There is a neuroanatomical functional divergence in the energy-intake- versus energy-metabolic features of CCKergic neurotransmission within the brain, with CCKNTS neurons modulating food intake, but not glucose homeostasis.
source: These results reveal a neuroanatomical functional divergence in the energy-intake- versus energy-metabolic features of CCKergic neurotransmission within the brain, with CCKNTS neurons modulating food intake, but not glucose homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing CCKNTS effects (no glucose effect) with CCKPBN effects (glucose regulation) from previous studies.

claim: Repeated activation of CCKNTS neurons resulted in a pronounced reduction in food intake with a concomitant reduction in body weight.
source: Repeated activation of CCKNTS neurons resulted in a pronounced reduction in food intake with a concomitant reduction in body weight (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by repeated CNO administration experiments over 4 days (Figure 2J).

claim: Following withdrawal of CNO treatment, mice returned to the original body weight within approximately 48 hr and to baseline food intake after a transient phase of rebound feeding.
source: Following withdrawal of CNO treatment, mice returned to the original body weight within approximately 48 hr and to baseline food intake after a transient phase of rebound feeding (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by body weight and food intake measurements following CNO withdrawal (Figure 2J).

claim: Sustained activation of CCKNTS neurons is sufficient to promote pronounced and reversible anorexia and body weight loss in mice.
source: These data demonstrate that sustained activation of CCKNTS neurons is sufficient to promote pronounced and reversible anorexia and body weight loss in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the repeated CNO administration experiments.

claim: Activation of CCKNTS neurons promotes anorexia and weight loss, attenuating the homeostatic drive to eat even in face of marked negative energy balance.
source: Together, these data reveal that activation of CCKNTS neurons promotes anorexia and weight loss, attenuating the homeostatic drive to eat even in face of marked negative energy balance (as occurs in food deprivation).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the feeding suppression experiments in both fed and fasted conditions.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of CCKNTS neurons elicited striking c-Fos-IR in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH) in food-deprived mice compared with saline-treated mice.
source: Chemogenetic activation of CCKNTS neurons elicited striking c-Fos-IR in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH) in food-deprived mice compared with saline-treated mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by c-Fos immunoreactivity data in the PVH following CNO administration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: The PVH represents a crucial hub for the brain's regulation of energy balance and integrates a diverse range of nutritionally related hormonal and synaptic inputs, including inputs from the NTS.
source: The PVH represents a crucial hub for the brain's regulation of energy balance and integrates a diverse range of nutritionally related hormonal and synaptic inputs, including inputs from the NTS (Grill and Hayes, 2012; Riche et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CCKNTS neurons directly innervate the PVH.
source: To evaluate whether CCKNTS neurons directly innervate the PVH, a Cre-inducible AAV vector expressing Channelrhodopsin-2-eYFP (ChR2-eYFP) was stereotaxically injected into the NTS of Cck-iCre mice (Figure 3A,B). Cre-mediated recombination of the vector led to expression of eYFP in CCKNTS cells and their projection fields (due to axonal localization of the ChR2-eYFP fusion protein), revealing robust CCKNTS → PVH innervation (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by anterograde tracing showing ChR2-eYFP-labeled CCKNTS axons in the PVH (Figure 3C).

claim: CCKNTS efferent projections innervate the ventral and more caudal aspect of the dorsomedial nucleus of the hypothalamus and, to a lesser extent, the arcuate nucleus.
source: CCKNTS efferent projections were also observed to innervate the ventral and more caudal aspect of the dorsomedial nucleus of the hypothalamus and, to a lesser extent, the arcuate nucleus (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: Supported by anterograde tracing images showing projections to these regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F).

claim: In vivo photostimulation of CCKNTS axon terminals in the PVH elicited c-Fos-IR in PVH neurons in close proximity of transduced CCKNTS axons.
source: In vivo photostimulation of CCKNTS axon terminals in the PVH elicited c-Fos-IR in PVH neurons in close proximity of transduced CCKNTS axons (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by c-Fos immunoreactivity data following optogenetic stimulation (Figure 3F).

claim: Optogenetic activation of the CCKNTS→PVH circuit produced an almost complete, and reversible, suppression of spontaneous feeding.
source: Monitoring home-cage food intake revealed that optogenetic activation of the CCKNTS→PVH circuit produced an almost complete, and reversible, suppression of spontaneous feeding (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by food intake measurements during optogenetic stimulation (Figure 3G).

claim: Optogenetic activation of the CCKNTS→PVH pathway neither suppresses locomotor activity nor water consumption.
source: Importantly, optogenetic activation of the CCKNTS→PVH pathway neither suppresses locomotor activity (Figure 3H) nor water consumption (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity and water consumption measurements during optogenetic stimulation (Figure 3H, 3I).

claim: Real-time optogenetic stimulation of the CCKNTS→PVH circuit significantly suppressed re-feeding in food deprived Cck-iCre-ChR2-eYFPNTS mice.
source: Furthermore, real-time optogenetic stimulation of this circuit (10 ms, 30 Hz, 1 s on, every 4 s) significantly suppressed re-feeding in food deprived Cck-iCre-ChR2-eYFPNTS mice (Figure 3J), but not control Cck-iCre-eYFPNTS mice (Figure 3K).
evidence: Supported by food intake measurements during optogenetic stimulation in fasted mice (Figure 3J, 3K).

claim: The reduction in food intake in Cck-iCre-ChR2-eYFPNTS stimulated mice was blunted by pre-treatment with the CCK-A receptor antagonist devazepide.
source: The reduction in food intake in Cck-iCre-ChR2-eYFPNTS stimulated mice was blunted by pre-treatment with the CCK-A receptor antagonist devazepide (Figure 3J)
evidence: Supported by food intake measurements following devazepide pre-treatment during optogenetic stimulation (Figure 3J).

claim: Optogenetic activation of CCKNTS→PVH efferent reduced the total number of chocolate pellets consumed.
source: Optogenetic activation of CCKNTS→PVH efferent reduced the total number of chocolate pellets consumed (Figure 3L)
evidence: Supported by chocolate pellet consumption measurements during optogenetic stimulation (Figure 3L).

claim: The appetite-suppressing properties of the CCKNTS→PVH circuit maintains salience even when the homeostatic drive to eat following food deprivation is boosted with a hedonic component.
source: indicating that the appetite-suppressing properties of the CCKNTS→PVH circuit maintains salience even when the homeostatic drive to eat following food deprivation is boosted with a hedonic component.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the chocolate pellet consumption experiment showing reduced intake despite hedonic value.

claim: Converging pharmacological and genetic data has established the importance of melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R)-expressing neurons in the regulation of energy balance.
source: Converging pharmacological and genetic data has established the importance of melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R)-expressing neurons in the regulation of energy balance (Fan et al., 1997; Huszar et al., 1997; Krashes et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The PVH has been identified as a principal site of MC4R satiety-promoting action.
source: with the PVH having been identified as a principal site of their satiety-promoting action (Balthasar et al., 2005; Garfield et al., 2015; Shah et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CCKNTS→PVH mCherry-positive fibers and varicosities are in close apposition to MC4R-expressing neurons.
source: We observed CCKNTS→PVH mCherry-positive fibers and varicosities in close apposition to MC4R-expressing neurons (Figure 3M and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing CCKNTS fibers near MC4R-GFP neurons (Figure 3M).

claim: Approximately 23% of PVH MC4R-expressing neurons were excited by CCK-8 application.
source: Moreover, using patch clamp electrophysiology, we observed that approximately 23% (5/23 cells) of PVH MC4R-expressing neurons were excited by CCK-8 application (Figure 3N).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings from MC4R-GFP neurons (Figure 3N).

claim: Cckar mRNA is expressed in 27% of MC4R PVH cells analyzed by single-cell qPCR.
source: Single-cell qPCR of manually sorted PVH Mc4r-t2a-Cre::tdTomato-expressing neurons revealed Cckar mRNA to be expressed in 27% (4/15) of MC4R PVH cells analyzed (Figure 3O and Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by single-cell qPCR data from Mc4r-t2a-Cre::tdTomato neurons (Figure 3O).

claim: Approximately 30% of PVH Mc4r-t2a-Cre::tdTomato neurons were excited by CCK-8 application, in a CCK-A receptor-dependent manner.
source: Likewise, electrophysiological recordings revealed that approximately 30% (6/20 cells) of PVH Mc4r-t2a-Cre::tdTomato neurons were excited by CCK-8 application, in a CCK-A receptor-dependent manner (0/11 cells; Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings from Mc4r-t2a-Cre::tdTomato neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).

claim: CCK is a novel peptide neurotransmitter activating the appetite-controlling PVH MC4R neurons.
source: Thereby, these data identify CCK as a novel peptide neurotransmitter activating the appetite-controlling PVH MC4R neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiology and single-cell qPCR data showing CCK activates MC4R neurons.

claim: The NTS is associated with negative valance and anorexia related to nausea.
source: In addition to the homeostatic regulation of energy balance, the NTS is also associated with negative valance and anorexia related to nausea (Lachey et al., 2005; Rinaman, 2004; Swank and Bernstein, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: No place preference was observed when Cck-iCre-ChR2-eYFPNTS or Cck-iCre-eYFPNTS controls were tested under normal energy balance conditions.
source: We observed no place preference when Cck-iCre-ChR2-eYFPNTS or Cck-iCre-eYFPNTS controls were tested under normal energy balance conditions, an important indication that activation NTSCCK→PVH efferents is not aversive (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Supported by real-time place preference test data in fed mice (Figure 4A-C).

claim: Activation of NTSCCK→PVH efferents is not aversive.
source: We observed no place preference when Cck-iCre-ChR2-eYFPNTS or Cck-iCre-eYFPNTS controls were tested under normal energy balance conditions, an important indication that activation NTSCCK→PVH efferents is not aversive (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of place preference in fed mice.

claim: Calorie depleted Cck-iCre-ChR2-eYFPNTS mice exhibited a significant preference for the photostimulation-paired chamber.
source: However, while Cck-iCre-eYFPNTS controls maintained no chamber preference when food deprived, calorie depleted Cck-iCre-ChR2-eYFPNTS mice exhibited a significant preference for the photostimulation-paired chamber (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Supported by real-time place preference test data in food-deprived mice (Figure 4B,C).

claim: Over the three testing trials Cck-iCre-ChR2-eYFPNTS mice developed a clear preference for the photostimulation-paired arm in a T-maze test.
source: Over the three testing trials Cck-iCre-ChR2-eYFPNTS mice, but not Cck-iCre-eYFPNTS controls, developed a clear preference for the photostimulation-paired arm (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Supported by T-maze test data showing increased time in photostimulation-paired arm (Figure 4E,F).

claim: When hungry and in the absence of food, mice sought out activation of the NTSCCK efferent to PVH, revealing the CCKNTS→PVH circuit encodes positive valence.
source: Thus, when hungry and in the absence of food, mice sought out activation of the NTSCCK efferent to PVH, revealing the CCKNTS→PVH circuit encodes positive valence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the place preference and T-maze data in food-deprived mice.

claim: The activation of the CCKNTS→PVH circuit provides relief from the unpleasantness of energy deficit by mimicking a post-prandial phase.
source: These data suggest that the activation of this circuit provides relief from the unpleasantness of energy deficit by mimicking a post-prandial phase.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the positive valence data in food-deprived mice.

claim: Activation of CCKNTS produces a prolonged effect on appetite and a rapid reduction in body weight.
source: While further studies attempting site-specific Cck loss of function are needed to fully clarify the physiological necessity of NTS CCKergic transmission in eating behavior and body weight regulation, here we reveal that activation of CCKNTS produces a prolonged effect on appetite and a rapid reduction in body weight.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the chemogenetic activation experiments.

claim: The reduction in energy intake due to CCKNTS activation is not due to an aversive state.
source: We did not find evidence that this reduction in energy intake is due to an aversive state
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of aversion in the place preference tests.

claim: The CCKNTS→PVH circuit transmits positive valence in an energy-state-dependent manner.
source: but rather, reveal that the CCKNTS→PVH circuit transmits positive valence in an energy-state-dependent manner
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the place preference data showing positive valence only in food-deprived mice.

claim: In patient populations the negative valence of energy deficit is a major factor contributing to low compliance on weight-loss diets.
source: a particularly attractive prospect considering that in patient populations the negative valence of energy deficit is a major factor contributing to low compliance on weight-loss diets.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about weight-loss diet compliance.

claim: Ex vivo application of blue light to CCKNTS neurons expressing ChR2 resulted in faithful action potential discharge with stimulation/discharge fidelity preserved at both 10 Hz and 30 Hz.
source: Ex vivo application of blue light (473 nm) to CCKNTS neurons expressing ChR2 using slice electrophysiology resulted in faithful action potential discharge with stimulation/discharge fidelity preserved at both 10 Hz and 30 Hz (but not 50 Hz, data not shown) in Cck-iCre-ChR2-eYFPNTS cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing light-evoked action potentials (Figure 3E).

claim: Parabrachial CCKergic (CCKPBN) transmission regulates hepatic glucose production.
source: Given our recent findings that parabrachial CCKergic (CCKPBN) transmission regulates hepatic glucose production (Flak et al., 2014; Garfield et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: CCKNTS neurons do not have substantial projections at other anterior hypothalamic regions besides the PVH.
source: revealing robust CCKNTS → PVH innervation (Figure 3C), with no substantial projections at other anterior hypothalamic regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by anterograde tracing images showing minimal projections to other anterior hypothalamic regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
